lessons.title: Open Outlook and find Mail and Calendar

sections.title: What Outlook is, and how you start it

blocks.html:
Microsoft Outlook is a program that keeps your email, calendars, contacts, tasks, and to-do lists in one place. Microsoft’s basic Outlook page (opened 10 November 2026) says your email account is the starting point. From there you can send and receive messages, turn a message into a task or an appointment, and store information about the people you write to so you do not have to remember every address.

This course teaches everyday workplace habits in Outlook, from finding Mail and Calendar through a simple appointment. It is not Microsoft Office Specialist (MOS) training, not college credit, and not legal advice. It does not replace *Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada*, which goes deeper into scams, or *Everyday Computers and Smartphones*, which covers the Start menu, locking a shared computer, and signing out. Longer writing craft belongs in *Workplace Writing*.

Canada’s Skills for Success Digital skill (learning-steps page opened 10 November 2026) includes using online tools such as email, and knowing how to avoid phishing emails. You will practise those ideas here. Lesson 6 stays basic and then points you to the email-safety course for more.

To start Outlook on a Windows computer, use the Start menu the same way you start Word or Excel. Everyday Computers covers that menu in more detail. The first time Outlook opens on a computer, Microsoft says Auto Account Setup may ask for your name, email address, and a password. That is usually enough. If automatic setup fails, Outlook may ask for extra details such as a mail server name, which your email provider can give you. Later you can choose File > Add Account to add another account.

Do not type a real workplace password into this course. Use a tutor-approved practice account, or watch a tutor demonstrate setup. Practice screens here are drawings labelled “Practice screen — not the real Outlook.”

Outlook does not look the same everywhere. Microsoft publishes steps for classic Outlook, new Outlook, Outlook on the web, and mobile apps. This course teaches the desktop steps Microsoft publishes. If a label on your screen does not match, ask a tutor rather than guessing at a reset.

sections.title: Find Mail, Calendar, People, and Tasks

blocks.html:
Once Outlook is open, look for a short list of the main areas: Mail, Calendar, People, and Tasks. Microsoft calls this the quick access bar on some screens and talks about a Navigation bar on others. The idea is the same: those four names move you among the top features. They often sit along the bottom or the side of the window. On a phone or in the new Outlook, the same names may appear as icons. If you cannot find Calendar, look along the bottom edge and the left edge before you assume it is missing.

Mail is where you read and write messages. New messages usually arrive in the Inbox, which Microsoft names as a mail folder you can work from. Calendar is where you see your time and add appointments or meetings — you will do that in Lesson 7. People is the place for contacts, and Tasks is the place for to-do items. Both wait until Lesson 8. You only need to know they exist today so you do not hunt for a calendar inside a single email.

Click Mail when you want your messages. Click Calendar when you want your schedule. Switching does not delete your mail. It only changes what you are looking at. If you clicked Calendar by mistake and your Inbox seems to have disappeared, click Mail again.

On many desktop screens, Mail itself has three parts. A folder list on the left shows Inbox and other folders — Lesson 5 will teach you how to make a folder. A message list shows subjects and senders. A reading pane, a name Microsoft uses on its reply page, can show the contents of the message you selected. If the reading pane is empty, click a message in the list. You do not have to reply yet.

If someone else uses the same library computer, sign out when you finish, the way Everyday Computers teaches for a shared machine. Do not leave Outlook open on a public desk.

sections.title: Look around without sending yet

blocks.html:
Today’s goal is to look around without sending anything. Opening Outlook is not the same as sending a message. You can read, switch to Calendar, and leave again without writing to anyone.

Microsoft’s first mail task is creating a new message with New Email, which you will do in Lesson 2. Today, notice where that command will live: from any mail folder, such as your Inbox, you choose New Email. You do not need to press it yet. Noticing the button now means you will not search the whole window later.

Also notice what you should not do on a first look. Do not type a real password into a practice screen. Do not open an unexpected attachment “just to see” — Lesson 4 and Lesson 6 cover attachments and suspicious mail. Do not choose Reply All on a large group while you are still learning the difference; that choice waits until Lesson 3. Curiosity is good. Clicking every button is not.

If setup asked for extra server details you do not have, stop and ask staff or your email provider. Guessing at server names can lock you out of a real account. That is another reason this course uses a practice account.

Write down the four names — Mail, Calendar, People, and Tasks — in your own words. If your screen uses icons only, ask a tutor to help you match each icon to a name. Screens differ by version. A library machine may show classic Outlook while a workplace laptop shows the new Outlook. Both can still get you to Mail and Calendar.

When you know those two places, you are ready to write a clear message in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Write and send a clear message

sections.title: Start a new message

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s basic Outlook page (opened 10 November 2026) says you create a new email from any mail folder, such as your Inbox, by choosing New Email. The keyboard shortcut Microsoft lists is Ctrl+Shift+M. When you are done composing, you choose Send.

Open Mail first so you can see the Inbox. Then choose New Email. A blank message window opens. It has a place for recipients, a subject line, and a large area for the words you want to send. Screens differ in classic Outlook, new Outlook, the web, and mobile apps, but those three parts are the ones you need today: who the message is for, what it is about, and what you want to say.

In the To box, type the address of the person who must read and act on the message. For practice, use the sample names in Outlook-Workplace-Sample-Messages-Sample-Only.txt, such as Jordan Lee at the Sampletown address we wrote. Do not send practice messages to a real workplace inbox unless your tutor says the practice account is set up for that.

Leave Cc and Bcc for Lesson 3. Today you are sending a simple note to one person. If you click New Email by mistake, close the window and choose No if Outlook asks whether to save a draft — or save the draft if you want to come back. Closing without Send does not deliver the message.

Use a tutor-approved practice account. Never type a real workplace password into this course. The practice screens are drawings labelled “Practice screen — not the real Outlook.” They will ask you to tap New Email and Send, not to hand over a password.

If New Email does not appear where you expect, look at the top of the Mail view. Microsoft says you start from any mail folder, so make sure you are in Mail and not in Calendar. Lesson 1 showed that switching views changes what you see; it does not create a new message for you.

sections.title: Write a subject and a short body

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s page on writing great email (opened 10 November 2026) says the key is to empathize with your recipients. Start with the subject. Make it descriptive and action-oriented so the other person can tell what the message is about before they open it. Microsoft’s example names a group and an action, such as asking managers to send dates. Useful prefixes include FYI: when the note is only for information and Action Required when the person must do something.

A subject such as “Question” or “Hi” does not help. “Saturday hall setup — can you confirm by Thursday?” tells Jordan what the note is about and what you need. If you are answering someone later in a long thread and the topic has changed, Microsoft says to change the subject. You will use Reply in Lesson 3; the same subject rule still applies.

Keep the body short and to the point. Organize the content from most important to least. Put questions or action items on separate lines so they stand out. Microsoft also suggests considering bold for important information, and putting people who must respond on the To line — which is where your one recipient belongs today.

Write the way you would speak politely at a front desk. Use Canadian spelling (*centre*, *colour*, *practise* as a verb). You do not need fancy stationery, unusual fonts, or a long story about your morning. If you cannot give a full answer yet, Microsoft says to let the sender know you are looking into the issue and will respond by a certain time. That habit also works when you are the one writing first: if you still need a fact, say so and name when you will follow up.

Read the message before you send it. Microsoft lists that as the first “do.” A thirty-second read catches a missing date, a wrong name, or a sentence that sounds sharper than you meant.

sections.title: Send the message, then check that it went

blocks.html:
When the To line, the subject, and the body look right, choose Send. Microsoft’s basic steps end there: compose, then Send. You do not need extra buttons for a simple practice note.

After you send, look for the message in Sent Items if your screen shows that folder. Microsoft’s Bcc page (opened 10 November 2026) notes that sent messages are stored by default in the Sent Items folder in classic Outlook for Windows. If you do not see Sent Items, ask a tutor — folder names can differ slightly, and you should not invent a second send “just in case.” Sending twice can confuse the other person.

If you realize you forgot a sentence, you can send a short follow-up. Microsoft warns against expecting a quick response to a long message and against sending a follow-up less than a day after the first note. For a missing time or a missing attachment (Lesson 4), a brief second message is kinder than silence. For “did you see my email?” sent ten minutes later, wait or use a phone call if you need an immediate answer. Microsoft says that if you want an immediate response, email is not the best tool — phone or an instant message can be clearer.

Do not mark every new message as High Importance. Microsoft says to use that marking sparingly, because people learn to ignore it. A clear subject does more work than a red exclamation mark.

Save a draft if you are not ready to send. Coming back to a draft is safer than sending an unfinished note, especially if you feel rushed. Lesson 4 will add tone and attachments. Today, a clear To line, a clear subject, a short body, and Send are enough.

lessons.title: Reply, Reply All, Forward, and To / Cc / Bcc

sections.title: Reply, Reply All, and Forward

blocks.html:
When a message arrives, Microsoft’s reply page (opened 10 November 2026) lists three everyday actions.

Reply sends your new message only to the original sender. Attachments are not included. Use Reply when your answer is meant for that one person — for example, telling Jordan you can help on Saturday.

Reply All sends your new message to the original sender and to everyone else on the To and Cc lines. Attachments are not included. Use Reply All only when the whole group needs your words. A line such as “I can bring two chairs” helps everyone planning the market. A question about your own shift usually does not.

Forward lets you type a whole new set of recipients. Any attachments that came with the original message are included automatically. Use Forward when you need to send the note to someone who was not on the To or Cc lines — for example, sending Sam’s heater note to a maintenance lead and adding one sentence of context.

Microsoft says you can find Reply, Reply All, and Forward in more than one place: at the top of the reading pane, beside the message, or on the main Outlook ribbon, depending on your screen and version. Choose the action first, then write your words, then choose Send.

Think before you choose Reply All. Microsoft asks you to consider whether everyone needs your reply, especially if the message went to many people or to a distribution list. It is often better to choose Reply and then add only the people you really want to include. If you already chose Reply All, you can still remove people who do not need the message before you send.

Never use Reply All on a large group only to ask to be removed. Microsoft’s writing-advice page says not to do that — ever. Ask the list owner or your administrator instead.

sections.title: Subjects, attachments, and a new set of names

blocks.html:
When you reply, Outlook sets the subject to start with RE: in front of the original subject. When you forward, the subject starts with FW:. Microsoft says you can leave that as it is, or type a new subject. If the topic has changed, change the subject so later readers are not misled.

Attachments behave differently, and this surprises many learners. When you reply or reply all, attachments are not included. Microsoft explains why: you would be sending the same file back to the person who just sent it to you. There is no setting that changes this. After you choose Reply or Reply All, you can attach a new version of the file or another file if you need to (Lesson 4). If you need someone new to receive the original attachments, use Forward. Forward includes those files automatically, and you can add more.

You can add or remove names in the To, Cc, and Bcc boxes after you choose Reply, Reply All, or Forward. To add someone, click in the box and type a name or address. To remove someone, select the name and press Delete.

If you want to send two or more messages to the same people as one note, Microsoft says to select the messages in the list (select the first, then hold Ctrl as you select the others) and then choose Forward on the main ribbon. The other messages are included as attachments. That is useful when a tutor asks you to pass along a short thread. It is not an excuse to forward a whole inbox.

Write a short line of your own when you forward. “Please see Sam’s note below — the heater in Room 12 clicked off between 1:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m.” is clearer than an empty forward, which can look like you did not read the message.

sections.title: To, Cc, and Bcc

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s writing-advice page says to limit the people who receive a message to those who need to read it. Put people who need to respond or take action on the To line. Put people who need to be informed on the Cc line. Cc stands for a copy that others can see. If Morgan only needs to know that chairs are arranged, Morgan can sit on Cc while Jordan stays on To.

Bcc means blind carbon copy. When you put a name in Bcc, that person receives a copy, but other recipients do not see the name. Microsoft’s Bcc page (opened 10 November 2026) says other people who receive the message do not see whose address is on the Bcc line. If you are the recipient, you cannot see whether the sender added Bcc names. Only the sender can see those names, by opening the message in Sent Items.

The Bcc box is not always visible. In new Outlook, Microsoft’s steps are Options > Show fields > Show Bcc. In classic Outlook, if the message opens in a new window, choose Options > Bcc. If it opens in the reading pane, choose Bcc from the ribbon. After you turn Bcc on in new Outlook, it stays until you turn it off.

Use Bcc to protect privacy when many people should not see one another’s addresses, or to quiet a long group thread by moving extra names to Bcc and saying so in the message. Do not use Bcc to secretly show a manager a sensitive note. Microsoft warns that the Bcc recipient may not realize they were blind-copied and may reply to everyone, exposing the Bcc. That can look sneaky. Microsoft says to forward the message after you send it instead.

sections.title: Attach a file, then open or save one you receive

blocks.html:
To share a file, Microsoft’s basic Outlook page (opened 10 November 2026) says you can attach it to your message. You can also attach other Outlook items, such as messages, contacts, or tasks, but this lesson stays with an everyday file.

Start a new message, or open an existing one and choose Reply, Reply All, or Forward. In the message window, choose Message > Attach File. Then pick the file you want. Give the message a clear subject that mentions the file if that helps the reader, such as “Saturday market — chair-count list attached.” Write one sentence in the body that says what the file is and what you want the person to do with it. An empty message with only an attachment can look unfinished or, later, suspicious.

Microsoft also notes on its writing-advice page that sending a link can be better than sending a file when your workplace already stores the document in a shared place. This course still teaches Attach File for a file that lives on your computer. If staff ask you to use a shared folder instead, follow that workplace rule.

When someone sends you a file, you can open it from the reading pane or from an open message. Microsoft says that, depending on your version, there may be more than one way to open it, and that double-clicking the attachment is one way. After you view it, you can save it. Choose the attachment, then on the Attachments tab, in the Actions group, choose Save As. You can also right-click the attachment and choose Save As. If there is more than one file, Microsoft says you can save them as a group or one at a time.

Save practice files in the folder your tutor or library staff named, with a clear name such as saturday-chairs-practice. Do not type a password, a Social Insurance Number, or other private numbers into a file on a shared computer.

sections.title: Treat unexpected files with care, and add a simple signature

blocks.html:
Open unexpected attachments with care. A file you were not waiting for — especially one that asks you to “enable macros,” enter a password, or visit a strange link — is a warning sign, not a homework task. Lesson 6 covers junk and phishing, and *Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada* goes further. Today’s rule is simple: if you were not expecting the file, do not open it just to see what happens. Ask staff or your tutor. Reply and Forward treat attachments differently, as you learned in Lesson 3: Reply does not send the original files back, and Forward does.

A signature is a short block of text that can appear at the bottom of your messages. Microsoft says signatures can include text, images, an electronic business card, a logo, or even a picture of a handwritten signature. For workplace mail, less is better. Microsoft’s writing-advice page says to use a signature when it is appropriate, and to keep it simple, short, professional, and, if possible, free of graphics.

To create one, Microsoft’s basic page says: in a new message, choose Signature > Signatures. On the Email Signature tab, choose New, type a name, and choose OK. Under Choose default signature, pick the account, then choose whether the signature is added automatically to new messages and, separately, to replies and forwards. The default for those lists can be (none). Under Edit signature, type the text, then choose OK. To add a signature by hand, choose Signature in a new message and pick the name you created.

A good practice signature for this course is two or three lines: your name, your role, and the organization — for example, “Alex Rivera, Weekend volunteer, Sampletown Community Centre.” Leave out large logos, colourful quotations, and personal slogans. Those can distract the reader and may not display well on a phone.

sections.title: Check the tone before you send

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s writing-advice page (opened 10 November 2026) is a list of professional do’s and don’ts. You already practised some of them in Lesson 2: read the message before you send it, write a descriptive subject, keep the note short, put the most important point first, and put questions on their own lines.

Add these tone habits today. Do not send a message while you are angry. Microsoft says it is better to write it, save it to your Drafts folder, and come back later. Do not write in ALL CAPS — it can look like shouting. Do not use sarcasm, because your humour may be misunderstood. Do not write something you would not want everyone at your workplace to read; you never know where a message might end up. Do not put your manager on every message you send. Do not mark every message High Importance, or people will learn to ignore the mark.

If you cannot give a full answer yet, send a short note that you are looking into the issue and will reply by a certain time. Flag the message for yourself if you need a reminder (Lesson 5). If a conversation has more than about ten messages without a resolution, Microsoft says to consider a call or a meeting. Email is not always the best tool for a tangled problem, and it is not the best tool when you need an immediate answer.

Use the tone checklist practice file as you reread. It turns Microsoft’s advice into boxes you can tick. Canadian spelling still matters: write *centre* and *colour* in the body, and keep the greeting and closing polite and plain.

sections.title: Create a folder and file a message

blocks.html:
Folders give you a place to keep related messages together. Microsoft’s folder page (opened 10 November 2026) says folders can organize email, calendars, contacts, and tasks. Today you will make one mail folder for a project — for practice, something like Saturday market — and put matching messages in it.

The words on the screen depend on your version. In new Outlook, Microsoft says to right-click your email address in the folder pane on the left (or hover and choose More options) and choose Create new folder, then type a name and press Enter. To make a folder inside another folder, right-click that folder and choose Create new subfolder. In classic Outlook, right-click in the left pane of Mail where you want the folder and choose New Folder, type a name, and press Enter. Outlook on the web and Outlook.com use similar “create new folder” steps. If the label you see is slightly different, ask a tutor rather than guessing at a reset.

Name the folder for the work it holds, not for the word “Stuff.” Saturday-market or Hall booking is easier to scan later than New folder. You do not need a dozen empty folders on the first day. One folder you will actually open is enough practice.

To put a message in the folder, Microsoft’s move page (opened 10 November 2026) gives two everyday methods that work in both new and classic Outlook. Select the message, drag it onto the destination folder, and release the mouse button. Or select the message and, on the ribbon in the Move group, choose Move, then pick the folder. You can also right-click the message and look for Move. If the folder is not in the short list, Microsoft says to choose the “different folder” or Other Folder option and pick it from the full list.

Filing is not the same as deleting. The message should still be there when you open the folder. If you cannot find it, look in Inbox and in the new folder before you assume it is gone.

sections.title: Flag a message you must follow up

blocks.html:
A folder keeps a topic together. A flag marks a message you still need to do something about — reply by Thursday, bring chairs, or check a heater note. Microsoft’s page on categories, flags, or reminders (opened 10 November 2026) says to select the flag icon on an email to make it a to-do item. The flag turns red.

For more detail, right-click the flag. Choose Add Reminder to open the menu. In the Custom box, for Flag to, you can select Follow up or type a short description. Check the Reminder box, pick a date and time, then choose OK. An alarm-bell icon appears on the message. Reminders show in the message list and the reading pane.

To see all follow-up flags, Microsoft says to choose View > Layout > To-Do Bar > Tasks. The To-Do Bar opens and lists the flags. When you finish the follow-up, right-click the message and choose Follow Up > Mark Complete. The flag changes to a green checkmark and the item leaves the To-Do Bar.

You can also add a category by right-clicking a message and choosing Categorize. Microsoft notes that the first time you use a category, Outlook may ask if you want to rename it; otherwise it is named for a colour (the menu may say Color). Categories are only seen by you. They are optional today. A red flag plus a clearly named folder already gives you two ways to find the work again.

Do not flag every message, just as you do not mark every message High Importance. If everything is flagged, nothing stands out. Flag the notes that need a next step.

sections.title: Search when you cannot remember the folder

blocks.html:
Even a neat folder list cannot replace search when you remember only a word or a sender. Microsoft’s search page (opened 10 November 2026) says the search box sits at the top of the Outlook window. Click it and type a word or phrase. Outlook scans email messages and many types of attachments. A search for chairs can find a message that mentions chairs in the subject, the body, or even some attached files.

You can narrow a search with short keywords. To find messages from one person, type from: and then the address, such as from:jordan.lee@sampletown-centre.example. To find a message by subject, search for a few words from that subject rather than the whole line. Microsoft’s example is that a long subject is easier to find if you search for two or three of its words. Punctuation is ignored, so a period at the end of a phrase does not change the results.

If the list is long, make the search more specific. Microsoft notes that Outlook returns only the first 1,000 search results so the program keeps running smoothly (page opened 10 November 2026). If the message you want is not in that list, add a sender, a subject word, or both.

Search does not replace careful filing, and filing does not replace search. Use both. When you have filed Saturday’s notes and flagged the one that needs a reply, you can find them again next week without scrolling the whole Inbox.

lessons.title: Spot junk and phishing without panicking

sections.title: Junk mail is not the same as a phishing trap

blocks.html:
Outlook tries to keep unwanted mail out of your Inbox. Microsoft’s junk-email page (opened 10 November 2026) says mail identified as possible junk can be moved automatically to the Junk Email folder, and that any malware — potentially harmful software or code — is disabled. That folder is worth a calm look, because a real message can land there by mistake — do not click every link “just in case.”

If you keep getting unwanted mail from the same address, Microsoft describes a blocked-senders list. In the view that page covers (new Outlook and similar web views), you open Settings, then Mail > Junk email, and add an address or a whole domain to Blocked senders and domains. Messages from those senders go to Junk Email. You can also add a person or domain to Safe senders so their mail is less likely to be treated as junk. The exact Settings labels can differ in classic Outlook. Ask a tutor if you cannot find Junk email.

Microsoft’s junk page opened on 10 November 2026 said junk is kept for 30 days and then deleted automatically. That detail can change, so check the folder sooner rather than later.

Phishing is different from ordinary junk. Junk is often advertising you did not ask for. Phishing is a message that tries to trick you into clicking a link, opening a file, or giving away a password, a PIN, or other private details. Canada’s Skills for Success Digital skill includes knowing how to avoid phishing emails. Get Cyber Safe, a Government of Canada site, says cyber criminals often use fear or intimidation, and that it can be hard to tell a real message from a scam — which is what the sender is counting on.

Deeper scam practice belongs in *Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada*. Today you learn how to pause inside Outlook so you do not panic and click.

sections.title: Look before you click

blocks.html:
Get Cyber Safe’s page “What to do about a suspicious-looking message” (opened 10 November 2026) offers a simple set of questions. Do you even have an account with the organization named in the message? If you do not, Get Cyber Safe says it is a phishing or scam message and you should delete it. If you do, check whether the sender’s address matches who they claim to be, including the spelling of the domain. Look for spelling mistakes or blurry logos. Notice urgent or threatening language, such as a demand to act immediately or a threat to close an account. Notice odd requests, such as asking for personal information, demanding payment, or telling you not to use the official app or the number on your card.

Get Cyber Safe also flags generic greetings such as “Dear sir or madam,” mismatched domains (a “bank” writing from a free mail address, or a look-alike name that swaps a letter for a number), and unexpected attachments or links. If you are unsure about a link, Get Cyber Safe says to hover your mouse over it to see where it really goes — and not to open it if you suspect a scam. Even a “probably legitimate” message is safer if you open the organization’s official website yourself instead of clicking the link in the email.

The sample-messages file includes Message 4, a made-up practice phishing note, not from a real bank. The sender uses a zero in “acc0unts” and a strange domain. The subject says “Account Rest.” The body has typos, a 24-hour threat, and an odd order not to call the number on your card. Do not click the practice link or type a password — Message 4 is there so you can practise noticing the signs.

A Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre feature opened in October 2026 adds that a message can be well written and still be fraud. Slow down, and do not let urgency, fear, or excitement push you into a quick decision.

sections.title: What to do next, without panic

blocks.html:
If a message looks suspicious, pause. Do not click the link. Do not open an unexpected attachment. Do not reply with a password, a PIN, or a one-time code. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre says you should never give those secrets to an unsolicited contact. Verify an unexpected request using contact details you find yourself — the official website or a phone number you already trust — not the details printed in the message.

At work or on a practice account that belongs to an organization, tell staff or your tutor. Get Cyber Safe says that if you think you have been a victim on a work computer, you should report the incident to your organization right away. Workplace IT may also want you to report phishing inside Outlook; Get Cyber Safe notes that you can report phishing to Microsoft in Outlook.com or the Outlook app. Ask staff how your workplace wants that done. This lesson will not invent extra ribbon buttons we did not confirm on every version.

You can report fraud or cybercrime to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre whether you were tricked or you only witnessed the attempt. The CAFC report page (opened 10 November 2026) points to reportcyberandfraud.canada.ca and to a toll-free phone line, 1-888-495-8501. You may report anonymously online. If you have been a victim, the CAFC also says to contact your local police as soon as you can. Local police investigate; the CAFC keeps a central record that helps law enforcement. Phone hours are listed on that official page and can change, so check the page.

If you already clicked or shared details, Get Cyber Safe’s victim page says to contact your financial institution if money information was involved, change passwords on affected accounts, and report the incident. Ask a person you trust, and use the email-safety course for more practice.

Everyday Computers already covers locking a shared machine and signing out when you leave a library desk.

lessons.title: Calendar: appointments and a simple meeting

sections.title: An appointment is not the same as a meeting

blocks.html:
Microsoft’s basic Outlook page (opened 10 November 2026) treats appointments and meetings as different things, even though both live on your calendar.

An appointment is time you put on your own calendar that does not invite other people and does not reserve a resource such as a conference room or equipment. A quiet half hour to review Saturday market notes is an appointment. No one else needs an invitation. No room needs to be booked.

A meeting includes other people and can include resources such as conference rooms. A fifteen-minute briefing that asks Jordan to join you is a meeting. Microsoft says you will get responses to your meeting requests in your Inbox — Accept, Decline, or a similar reply, depending on what the other person chooses.

That difference saves embarrassment. If you use New Appointment for a briefing and never invite Jordan, Jordan will not know to come. If you use New Meeting for a private review hour and add half the building, you have turned quiet work time into a group event.

Switch to Calendar using the navigation you learned in Lesson 1. The calendar grid shows days and times. Screens differ in classic Outlook, new Outlook, the web, and mobile apps. The two commands you need today still have the same idea: New Appointment for your own time, and New Meeting when other people are part of the plan.

You do not need every calendar tool Microsoft offers. This lesson does not teach repeating events, room finders, or shared workplace calendars that your organization may manage differently. If staff use a shared calendar for vacations or hall bookings, follow their instructions. The calendar planning sheet for this course keeps you with one appointment and one simple meeting.

sections.title: Create an appointment

blocks.html:
In a Calendar folder, Microsoft says to choose New Appointment. You can also right-click a time block on the calendar grid and choose New Appointment. The keyboard shortcut Microsoft lists is Ctrl+Shift+A.

Give the appointment a clear title, the way you give an email a clear subject. “Review Saturday market notes” is more useful later than “Busy.” Set the date, the start time, and the end time. The practice sheet uses Wednesday, 12 November 2026, from 1:00 p.m. to 1:30 p.m. If you are working in a live practice account after that date, pick the next free half hour instead. Do not invite anyone and do not book a room. That is what makes it an appointment.

Set a reminder so the time does not slip by. Microsoft says to open the appointment (or meeting) and, in the Reminder list, choose how long before the event you want the reminder to appear. To turn a reminder off, choose None. The practice sheet suggests 15 minutes before.

Then save the item with the save control on your screen. The label can differ by version, so look for a save command rather than Send — you are not sending this appointment to other people. If you cannot find save, ask a tutor. After you save, you should see the title on the calendar grid at the right time.

If you created the item from the wrong button and it looks like a meeting, close it without sending an invite and start again with New Appointment. It is easier to begin once more than to send a meeting request you did not mean to send.

sections.title: Create a simple meeting

blocks.html:
When other people need to be there, choose New Meeting from a Calendar folder. Microsoft lists the shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Q, which creates a new meeting request from any folder in Outlook — even from Mail. That is handy if you are reading a thread and realize the group needs a short conversation instead of another long email. Microsoft’s writing-advice page said the same idea in reverse: after many messages without a resolution, consider a meeting.

Add a clear title, a date, and start and end times. The practice sheet uses “Saturday market briefing” on Thursday, 13 November 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 10:15 a.m. In the invite field, add the practice name Jordan Lee and the sample address from the sheet. Write one line in the body, such as “Confirm who is bringing extra chairs.” Set a reminder if you want one.

Then send the meeting request. Unlike an appointment, a meeting is meant to reach other people. Microsoft says replies arrive in your Inbox. In a tutor-approved practice account, you may not receive a real reply from Jordan — the address is sample only. The habit still matters: after you send a real meeting at work, watch the Inbox for responses instead of assuming everyone saw the invite.

Do not invite real coworkers from this course unless your tutor says the practice account is safe to use that way. Never type a real workplace password into the course. If your workplace uses extra meeting tools (a video link, a room list, or a required form), follow those workplace rules. This lesson stays with the basic Microsoft distinction: appointment for you, meeting for you and other people.

lessons.title: Contacts, tasks, and good daily habits

sections.title: People: save a name you will write to again

blocks.html:
People is Microsoft’s name for the contacts you keep in Outlook — persons and companies you write to. Microsoft’s basic page (opened 10 November 2026) says who you add is up to you, except for limits you or your organization set. A workplace may have rules about writing to certain outside addresses. Follow those rules. This lesson stays with one practice contact.

You will find Contacts under People on the shortcuts or navigation bar, often in the lower-left corner of the Outlook window, beside Mail, Calendar, and Tasks. In People, choose New Contact. The keyboard shortcut Microsoft lists is Ctrl+Shift+C, which works from any folder in Outlook.

A contact can be as simple as a name and an email address. You can also store street addresses, more than one phone number, a picture, and birthdays. For this course, a name and a practice email are enough. Use a sample such as Jordan Lee and jordan.lee@sampletown-centre.example. Do not store real personal details about coworkers in a shared-library file, and do not type a password or a Social Insurance Number into a contact card.

Save the contact with the save control on your screen. The next time you write a message, you can type the name on the To line instead of the whole address. That is the everyday payoff: fewer spelling mistakes on addresses you use often.

This course will not walk through exporting a contact list to a spreadsheet. Microsoft documents extra export steps that matter on someone else’s computer; skip those unless staff are helping you move a real address book. Contacts are a helpful extra here, not the heart of the course. Mail, tone, filing, safety, and the calendar still matter more.

sections.title: Tasks: a to-do item you can find again

blocks.html:
Many people keep to-do lists on paper, in a notebook, or in a mix of both. Microsoft says that in Outlook you can combine lists, get reminders, and track progress. Microsoft also invites you to try the To Do app to manage tasks. This lesson stays with a basic Outlook task so you are not learning a second program in the last chapter.

To create a task, Microsoft’s steps are: open Outlook and, on the Home tab, in the New group, choose New Items, then choose Task. Fill in the form as you need to, then choose Save & Close. The shortcut is Ctrl+Shift+K. You can also open Tasks on the navigation bar and start a task from there.

Give the task a clear subject, the way you title an email or an appointment: “Bring two extra chairs on Saturday” is better than “Chairs.” Add a due date if your form offers one. You can set a reminder on a task as well. Then save it. To view a task later, choose Tasks (or the To-Do List) on the navigation bar and double-click the item.

Outlook can also assign a task to another person; that request arrives in their Inbox. This course does not ask you to assign work to a classmate or a real coworker. Creating and finishing a task for yourself is enough. If your workplace uses assigned tasks or the To Do app every day, ask staff to show you their version after you finish this lesson.

A flag on an email (Lesson 5) and a task you create yourself can cover the same kind of follow-up. Use whichever you will actually look at tomorrow. Two overlapping lists that you never open are not more organized than one list you trust.

sections.title: A calmer workday in Outlook

blocks.html:
The course comes together as a short set of daily habits, not as a pile of extra buttons.

Start in Mail. Read new messages in the Inbox before you react. Choose Reply when only the sender needs your words, and Reply All only when the group needs them. Put people who must act on To and people who only need to know on Cc. Read once more before Send. Attach a file with a sentence that names it, and keep your signature simple.

File what you want to find again, and flag what still needs a next step. Use search — including from: plus an address — when you remember a sender but not a folder. Look at Calendar so today’s appointments and meetings are not a surprise. Create an appointment for your own time and a meeting when someone else must be there. Watch the Inbox for meeting replies.

If a message looks like junk or phishing, pause. Do not click. Do not send a password. Tell staff, use official contact details you find yourself, and report fraud to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre if you need to. More scam practice lives in *Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada*. On a shared computer, sign out the way Everyday Computers teaches.

None of this is MOS training, legal advice, or a promise that a tutor watched you work. The next step in this course is an ungraded capstone — one good workday checklist — and then a knowledge exam. Use a tutor-approved practice account until you are ready to apply the same habits in a real mailbox your organization gave you.

sections.title: Capstone

blocks.html:
This capstone sits after Lesson 8. It pulls the course together: you send one clear practice message, reply with care, file a message, and add one practice appointment.

This is not MOS training, not legal advice, and not a real workplace mailbox. Use the sample messages and the calendar planning sheet we wrote. Do not type a Social Insurance Number, a password, a real bank number, or anyone else’s private details. Use a tutor-approved practice account.

### What to build

  1. Open a tutor-approved practice account. Never type a real workplace password into this course.
  2. Choose New Email. Address a practice note to Jordan Lee (sample address). Write a descriptive subject and a short body. Read it once. Choose Send. Look in Sent Items if that folder appears.
  3. Open Message 1 or Message 2 from the sample file. Choose Reply or Reply All for the right reason, not by habit.
  4. Create a folder such as Saturday market if you do not already have one. Move at least one message into it (drag or Move). Flag a follow-up if something still needs a next step.
  5. Open Calendar and create Plan 1 from the calendar planning sheet as an appointment (no guests, no room). Set a reminder and save it.
  6. Optional extras: attach a harmless practice file and name it in the body; add a simple signature; save Jordan as a practice contact.
  7. Do not click Message 4. Do not invite real coworkers unless your tutor says the account is safe to use that way.
  8. Sign out if you are on a shared computer.
